To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

human cell extracts can incise DNA at multiple sites 5' to a G:T mismatch, that these incision events are stimulated by ATP and G: U DNA and that the multiple incision events at G:T are inhibited by an ApG/T mismatch.

human cell extract, in the presence of ATP, incises the model DNA at multiple sites on the same side and on opposite sides of the G:T mismatch, and that the ATP-dependent incision activity at a single G:T site is inhibited by the presence of an ApG/T mismatch.
human cell extracts show a multiplicity of strand incision events at a G:T mismatch, and this multiplicity is modified by the presence of a G:U mismatch.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the ATP-dependent G:U and G:T incision activities in human cell extracts.
the ATP-dependent G: T incision activity in the HT29 cell line and the possible involvement of the G:U mispairs in its modification.
the characterization of the multiple ATP-dependent incisions at a G:T mismatch in DNA by human cells, and we suggest a mechanism for the ATP-dependent G>T incision activity in human cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HT29 extract contains a modified single ATP-independent and ATP-dependent G:T misincision activity.

the HT29 extract contains a novel ATP-dependent incision activity, and that the MMR-defective HCT116 extract contains a modified ATP-dependent incision factor, which is required by the ATP-dependent G:U incision activity.

the human cell extract contains a modified TDG-like ATP-dependent activity that incises DNA at multiple sites around G:T base mismatch, and this incision activity is likely modified by the G:U mispairs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ATP-dependent G:U incision activity is modified by G:T mispair and that the ATP-dependent incision activity at a G:T mismatch in DNA is likely a modified single ATP-incision activity.
the ATP-dependent G:U incision activity is not a simple G:T mismatch incision activity.
multiple strand incision at a G:T mismatch is likely a consequence of the interaction between the ATP-dependent incision activity and G:U mispairs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
multiple ATP-dependent incisions at G:T base mispairs can be detected in human cell extracts, and the incision at a G:T mismatch is not a single event.

the human cell extracts, when supplemented with ATP, can carry out multiple ATP-dependent incisions at a G:T mismatch, and that the incision activity is modified by an interaction between the G:T mismatch and G:U mispairs.
the ATP-dependent G>T incision activity is a complex of multiple incision events, and it is modified by the presence of G:U mispairs.
